name: Williams Pointe
headline: Metro West Housing Solutions, Lakewood's housing authority, won a $1,430,242-a-year 2023 Round One 9% award for Williams Pointe, 44 family apartments (20% to 70% AMI) on a steep 2.2-acre hillside it owns at 1515 Whippoorwill Drive in Applewood, but the project did not proceed: CHFA's award report marks it with an asterisk whose footnote reads 'Project did not proceed. Award returned by sponsor.'
why_it_matters: It is a cautionary case of a by-right, sponsor-owned, low-land-cost 9% site failing on site cost and access: a hillside needing heavy grading and retaining walls, a single access route that neighbors and some planning commissioners called unsafe, a subdivision appeal and six rounds of site plan review, ending with the credits returned and the site plan withdrawn.

status.label: Did not proceed: award returned; site plan and building permit applications withdrawn
status.detail: CHFA's 2023 Round One award report (as of 2025-02-26) footnotes Williams Pointe: 'Project did not proceed. Award returned by sponsor.' A neighborhood group post dated 2025-01-05 says MWHS withdrew its major site plan application and canceled its building permit application, and quotes an MWHS email saying it would not complete financing of Williams Pointe that year and would work on temporary and permanent uses of the property. The date the credits were returned is not public, and the project no longer appears on MWHS's future communities page.

next_step: Watch Lakewood planning records and MWHS board materials for any new use or sale of 1515 Whippoorwill Drive, and CHFA applicant reports for a re-application.

key_numbers.value: $1,430,242 a year in federal 9% credit, returned
key_numbers.meaning: About $14.3M over 10 years (inferred) went back to CHFA; the award report footnote says the sponsor returned it.
Average 50% AMI, with 6 units at 20% AMI, which the applicant said would be the first 20% AMI units in its market area.
A Division of Housing loan of $4.4M and grant of $2.2M, as reported in September 2024 from a DOLA press release that could not be opened.
Lakewood's Planning Commission upheld the subdivision plat on 2024-08-21 after a five-and-a-half-hour hearing, per a resident news site; access safety stayed unresolved.

facts.value: 1515 Whippoorwill Drive, Lakewood, CO 80215 (just east of Colfax Avenue and Youngfield Street, Applewood area)
Two unplatted parcels owned debt-free by MWHS for nearly 20 years, platted into one 2.233-acre lot (Applewood Heights Filing No. 2); zoned for the use by right; not in a QCT or DDA
Two three-story wood-frame buildings on spread footings with retaining walls; flat TPO roofs; cold-climate heat pump PTACs; 8 covered stairways; Enterprise Green Communities 2020; all-electric ready
About 518 sq ft (studio), 613 (1BR), 892 (2BR) and 1,085 (3BR, two baths)
Part-time resident services coordinator paid by MWHS

Sole entrance and exit via Youngfield Street and W. 15th Place (about a 10% grade, per neighbors); neighbors pressed for access from Colfax Avenue, saying the city's 2014 plans for the same site had required Colfax access
Mixed Use Suburban; neighbors say the land was rezoned from R-1A in 2012. MWHS's brief cites City Council's decision to zone the property for the proposed use

background.text: The asterisk: CHFA's public 2023 Round One award report (as of 2025-02-26) marks Williams Pointe and Point of the Pines Villas with an asterisk, footnoted 'Project did not proceed. Award returned by sponsor.' The report still lists the original award amounts.

MWHS named the project for its first development director, William (Bill) Lunsford, who bought the parcel early in his tenure; at award MWHS expected to start construction in early 2024 and open in August 2025.

The application flagged the site as the largest cost driver: steep topography needing extensive grading and retaining walls, offset by the low land basis and a sizable MWHS cash contribution. The market analyst listed location as a minor weakness.

MWHS filed a minor subdivision application at the city's direction to combine the parcels into one lot; the Planning Director approved the plat on 2024-06-26; nearby residents appealed on 2024-07-10, arguing the city lacked authority, the plat improperly segmented the project and the decision was arbitrary. City staff recommended denying the appeal.

MWHS's hearing brief argued the appellants opposed affordable housing on the site, that old plat covenants had expired after 1974, and that tap fees of almost $500,000 could not be required just to create a lot.

The Planning Commission denied the appeal 4-2 on 2024-08-21; one commissioner said the plat met subdivision standards but the project as proposed most likely did not meet some site plan standards, citing the driveway slope and intersection.

According to the neighborhood group, MWHS's fifth site plan revision in fall 2024 did not change the access, and on 2024-10-24 Lakewood's mayor wrote to the group that added vehicle trips would likely make that stretch of road less safe and that she was working with staff on the project. The group says the project went through six major site plan reviews before MWHS withdrew the site plan and canceled the building permit application.
